title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Vronsky followed the guard to the carriage, and at the compartment door he stopped short to let a lady get out.

With the instinct of a man of the world, from one glance at this lady's appearance Vronsky classified her as belonging to the best society. He begged pardon and was about to get into the carriage when he felt he had to glance at her once more — not because she was very beautiful, not on account of the elegance and modest grace that were apparent in her whole figure, but because in the expression of her charming face, as she passed close by him, there was something especially caressing and soft. As he looked round, she too turned her head. Her shining gray eyes, which looked dark from the thick lashes, rested with friendly attention on his face, as if she were recognizing him, and then promptly turned away to the passing crowd, as though looking for someone. In that brief look Vronsky had time to notice the suppressed eagerness that played across her face and flickered between her brilliant eyes and the faint smile curving her red lips. It was as if her nature were so brimming over with something that against her will it showed itself now in the flash of her eyes, now in her smile. She deliberately shrouded the light in her eyes, but it shone against her will in that faintly perceptible smile.

Vronsky stepped into the carriage. His mother, a dried-up old lady with black eyes and ringlets, screwed up her eyes, looking her son over, and smiled slightly with her thin lips. Getting up from her seat and handing her maid a bag, she gave her son her little wrinkled hand to kiss, and lifting his head from her hand, kissed him on the cheek.
"You got my telegram? Quite well? Thank God."
"You had a good journey?" her son said, sitting down beside her and listening in spite of himself to a woman's voice outside the door. He knew it was the voice of the lady he had met at the door.
"All the same, I don't agree with you," the lady's voice was saying.
"It's the Petersburg view, madame."
"Not Petersburg, simply feminine," she replied.
"Well, well, let me kiss your hand."
"Good-bye, Ivan Petrovitch. And could you check whether my brother is here and send him to me?" said the lady from the doorway, and turned back into the compartment.
"Well, have you found your brother?" Countess Vronskaya said to the lady.
Vronsky now understood that this was Madame Karenina.
"Your brother is here," he said, standing up. "Excuse me, I didn't recognize you, and, indeed, our acquaintance was so brief," Vronsky said, bowing, "that no doubt you don't remember me."

"Oh, no," she said, "I should have known you because your mother and I have been talking, I think, of nothing but you the whole way." As she spoke she let the eagerness that insisted on showing itself break through in her smile. "And still no sign of my brother."
"Do call him, Alexey," said the old countess. Vronsky stepped out onto the platform and shouted:
"Oblonsky! Here!"

But Madame Karenina did not wait for her brother; catching sight of him, she stepped out with her light, decisive step. And as soon as her brother had reached her, with a gesture that struck Vronsky by its decision and its grace, she flung her left arm around his neck, drew him quickly to her, and kissed him warmly. Vronsky gazed, never taking his eyes off her, and smiled, he could not have said why. But remembering that his mother was waiting for him, he went back into the carriage.

"She's very sweet, isn't she?" said the countess of Madame Karenina. "Her husband put her in with me, and I was delighted to have her. We talked the whole way. And so you, I hear... _vous filez le parfait amour. Tant mieux, mon cher, tant mieux._"
"I don't know what you're referring to, maman," he answered coldly. "Come, maman, let's go."
Madame Karenina came back into the carriage to say good-bye to the countess.
"Well, countess, you've met your son and I my brother," she said. "And my gossip is all used up. I'd have nothing else to tell you now."

"Oh, no," the countess said, taking her hand. "I could travel right around the world with you and never be bored. You're one of those delightful women in whose company it's lovely to be silent as well as to talk. Now, please, don't fret over your son — you can't expect never to be parted."
Madame Karenina stood quite still, holding herself very straight, her eyes smiling.
"Anna Arkadyevna," the countess explained to her son, "has a little boy of eight, I believe, and she has never been parted from him before, and she keeps fretting over leaving him."
"Yes, the countess and I have been talking the whole time, I about my son and she about hers," said Madame Karenina, and again a smile lit up her face — a caressing smile meant for him.

"I'm afraid you must have been horribly bored," he said, picking up at once the little ball of flirtation she had tossed him. But evidently she did not care to pursue the conversation in that vein, and she turned to the old countess.
"Thank you so much. The time has passed so quickly. Good-bye, countess."
"Good-bye, my love," the countess answered. "Let me have a kiss of your pretty face. I speak plainly, at my age, and I tell you simply that I've lost my heart to you."

Stereotyped as the phrase was, Madame Karenina obviously believed it and was delighted by it. She flushed, bent down slightly, and pressed her cheek to the countess's lips, drew herself up again, and with the same smile fluttering between her lips and her eyes, gave her hand to Vronsky. He pressed the little hand she gave him, and was delighted, as if at something special, by the energetic squeeze with which she freely and vigorously shook his hand. She left with the rapid step that carried her rather fully developed figure with such strange lightness.
"Very charming," the countess said.

That was exactly what her son was thinking. His eyes followed her until her graceful figure was out of sight, and even then the smile stayed on his face. He saw through the window how she went up to her brother, slipped her arm through his, and began telling him something eagerly — obviously something that had nothing to do with him, Vronsky — and at that he felt annoyed.
"Well, maman, are you perfectly well?" he asked again, turning to his mother.
"Everything was delightful. Alexander was very good, and Marie has grown very pretty. She's very interesting."
And she began once more on the subject that most interested her — the christening of her grandson, which had kept her in Petersburg, and the special favor the Tsar had shown her elder son.
"Here's Lavrenty," said Vronsky, looking out of the window; "now we can go, if you like."
The old butler who had traveled with the countess came over to announce that everything was ready, and the countess rose to leave.
"Come — there's not such a crowd now," said Vronsky.

The maid took a handbag and the lap dog, the butler and a porter the rest of the luggage. Vronsky gave his mother his arm; but just as they were getting out of the carriage several men ran past with panic-stricken faces. The station-master ran by too in his oddly colored cap. Obviously something unusual had happened. The crowd who had left the train were running back.

"What?... What?... Where?... Threw himself!... Crushed!..." could be heard in the crowd. Stepan Arkadyevitch, with his sister on his arm, turned back. They too looked frightened and stopped at the carriage door to avoid the crowd.
The ladies got in, while Vronsky and Stepan Arkadyevitch followed the crowd to find out the details of the disaster.
A guard, either drunk or too heavily muffled up against the bitter frost, had not heard the train backing up and had been crushed.
Before Vronsky and Oblonsky came back, the ladies had heard the facts from the butler.
Oblonsky and Vronsky had both seen the mutilated body. Oblonsky was visibly shaken. He was frowning and seemed about to cry.
"Ah, how awful! Ah, Anna, if you had seen it! Ah, how awful!" he said.
Vronsky did not speak; his handsome face was serious but perfectly composed.

"Oh, if only you had seen it, countess," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "And his wife was right there... It was awful to see her — she threw herself onto the body. They say he was the sole support of a huge family. How awful!"
"Couldn't anything be done for her?" Madame Karenina said in an agitated whisper.
Vronsky glanced at her and at once got out of the carriage.
"I'll be right back, maman," he said, turning round in the doorway.

When he returned a few minutes later, Stepan Arkadyevitch was already in conversation with the countess about the new singer, while the countess was looking impatiently toward the door, waiting for her son.

"Now, let's be off," Vronsky said, coming in. They went out together. Vronsky walked in front with his mother. Behind came Madame Karenina with her brother. Just as they were leaving the station, the station-master overtook Vronsky.
"You gave my assistant two hundred roubles. Would you kindly say for whose benefit you intend the money?"
"For the widow," said Vronsky, shrugging. "I should have thought there was no need to ask."
"You gave that?" Oblonsky cried behind him, and, squeezing his sister's hand, he added, "Very nice, very nice! Isn't he a splendid fellow? Good-bye, countess."
And he and his sister stood waiting, looking for her maid.
When they came out, Vronsky's carriage had already driven away. People going in were still talking about what had happened.
"What a horrible death!" said a gentleman, passing by. "They say he was cut in two."
"On the contrary, I think it's the easiest — instantaneous," another observed.
"How is it they don't take proper precautions?" said a third.
Madame Karenina settled into the carriage, and Stepan Arkadyevitch saw with surprise that her lips were quivering and that she was struggling to hold back her tears.
"What is it, Anna?" he asked when they had driven a few hundred yards.
"It's an omen of evil," she said.
"What nonsense!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "You've arrived — that's the main thing. You can't imagine how much I'm counting on you."
"Have you known Vronsky long?" she asked.
"Yes. You know we're hoping he'll marry Kitty."

"Really?" Anna said softly. "Come now, let's talk about you," she added, tossing her head as if she would physically shake off something heavy weighing on her. "Let's talk about your affairs. I got your letter, and here I am."
"Yes, all my hopes are in you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Well, tell me all about it."
And Stepan Arkadyevitch began to tell his story.
On reaching home Oblonsky helped his sister out, sighed, pressed her hand, and set off for his office.
